title: Speed cameras at all school zones, transit fixes
subtitle: Also: Charles Street Terminal cleanup, GRT Route 34 extension, environmental grants, expropriations, and Fischer-Hallman left-turn request.
overview: The Planning and Works Committee recommended expanding automated speed enforcement to every school zone in the region, with 25 to 30 new zones each year from 2024 and all 175 schools covered by the end of 2028. The recommendation depends on 2024 budget approval. Councillors asked for revenue estimates before Council's June 21 meeting and for options using semi-fixed cameras.

The committee also recommended extending GRT Route 34 from September 5, 2023 to replace part of the discontinued Route 2, and adding iXpress stops at Highland and the walkway to Burnaby. Route 73 has no replacement. It recommended a municipally led site cleanup process for the Charles Street Terminal, and extending funding for the rare Charitable Research Reserve. It also supported 2023 environmental grants.

Several items were deferred or sent to staff. A developer's request for a left-turn lane on Fischer-Hallman Road will come back to Council with a staff report. A councillor's proposal on the countryside line was referred to staff for June 21. The committee received reports on the provincial decision on the Regional Official Plan, water capacity and Doon Heritage Village utilities.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended expanding speed cameras to all school zones, 25 to 30 new zones a year from 2024 with all 175 schools done by the end of 2028, subject to 2024 budget approval, plus criteria for community safety zones {{vote:m10}}.

The committee recommended extending Route 34 from September 5, 2023 and adding iXpress stops at Highland/Walkway to Burnaby, with $98,000 from the Tax Stabilization Reserve in 2023 and $294,000 in the 2024 budget {{vote:m11}}.
The committee recommended a municipally led Risk Assessment and Record of Site Condition process for contamination before any redevelopment proposal request {{vote:m9}}.
The committee recommended $103,795 for 20 projects, raising the Dog Strangling Vine response to $8,800 with the $3,795 increase from the operating budget {{vote:m8}}.
The committee recommended extending the funding agreement for five more years at $50,000 a year for 2023 to 2027.

decisions.item: Cedar Creek and Trussler roundabout expropriation
decisions.detail: The committee recommended expropriating land for a roundabout at Cedar Creek Road and Trussler Road in North Dumfries and Oxford County.
The committee recommended expropriating land on Northfield Drive West, Waterloo, to finish the remaining Farmers Market Trail works.
The committee recommended replacing the Level 1 crossover at Arthur and Mill Streets in Woolwich with an intersection pedestrian signal, and removing two non-existent crossovers from the by-law.

debate: On speed cameras, several councillors said they could not support such a large spending plan without revenue figures. Staff said costs are expected to be covered by revenue and promised a full business case in August. Others compared the cameras to seatbelt and smoking rules and said they are aimed at child safety.

Councillors questioned whether every school zone needs its own camera. Some suggested about 40 moved around. Staff said fixed sites reduce the work of moving cameras, but offered to report on semi-fixed options.

On Route 2 and 73, councillors said residents were not consulted before the routes were cut. Staff committed to broader rider consultation alongside the budget process. The Chair said Council chose the cuts in a hard election-year budget. Route 73 riders had no alternative, since it ran at peak times with few riders.

A developer asked for a left-turn lane into a grocery-anchored site on Fischer-Hallman Road, saying grocery tenants require it. Staff raised safety concerns about turning across two lanes and a multi-use trail. Some councillors did not want to build a median and later remove it. Others wanted more information, and staff said the work is not scheduled until mid-July.

On the Regional Official Plan decision, councillors raised concerns about debt and infrastructure costs. Staff said uncertainty over development charges after Bill 23 means property taxes and water rates are the only fallback if charges fall short.
